By the end of the lecture, you will be able to ...

-   Generate and communicate predictions from OLS regression models.

# Code-along 08 {data-menu-title="Code-along" background-image="images/terminal.png"}

Download and open [code-along-08.qmd](https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fi/tapnw643rp19don4z38qe/code-along-08.qmd?rlkey=654vq3lssf7zy4266veaqhway&st=vi14yolc&dl=1)

## Packages {.sparse-slide}

Load the standard packages.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| label: load

library(tidyverse) 
library(haven) # not core tidyverse
library(gssr)
library(gssrdoc)
library(summarytools)
library(gtsummary) 
library(modelbased)

```

## Load your data {.sparse-slide}

```{r}
#| message: false
#| label: gssdata

# Load GSS 2024
gss24 <- gss_get_yr(2024)

```

## Variables {.sparse-slide .smaller}

- `realrinc` R's income in constant \$
- `age` Age of respondent
- `educ` Respondents highest edu credit
- `hrs1` How many hours did you work last week
- `sex` Respondents sex
- `marital` R's marital status

##  {.smaller data-menu-title="Variable Management"}

::: task
{{< fa check-double >}} Make a df with only the (pretty) categorical and
continuous variables we'll analyze.
:::

```{r}
#| message: false
#| label: my-data

# Categorical Variables
my_cat <- gss24 |>
  select(id, sex, marital) |>
  zap_missing() |>
  mutate(
    sex = as_factor(sex),
    marital = as_factor(marital)) |> 
  droplevels()

# Continuous Variables
my_con <- gss24 |>
  select(id, age, educ, hrs1, realrinc) |>
  mutate(
    age = as.numeric(age),
    educ = as.numeric(educ),
    hrs1 = as.numeric(hrs1),
    realrinc = as.numeric(realrinc))

# Combine the two dataframes
my_data <- full_join(my_cat, my_con, by = c("id")) |> 
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(
    marital = recode(
      marital,
      "married"       = "Married",
      "never married" = "Never married",
      "widowed"       = "Div/Wid/Sep",
      "divorced"      = "Div/Wid/Sep",
      "separated"     = "Div/Wid/Sep"),
    marital = factor(
      marital,
      levels = c("Never married", "Div/Wid/Sep", "Married"))
  )

remove(my_con) # clean up the Environment
remove(my_cat)
```

# Predictions {.theme-section}

## {data-menu-title="Regression Model"}

OLS Regression Predicting Annual Income

```{r}
#| label: regress
#| echo: false

model <- lm(formula = realrinc ~ educ + hrs1 + sex + marital, data = my_data)

model |>
    tbl_regression(
    intercept = TRUE,
        show_single_row = sex,
    label = list(
      sex = "Women",
      marital = "Marital status (ref. = never married)")) |>
  remove_row_type(type = c("reference")) |>  
  modify_column_hide(conf.low) |>
  modify_column_unhide(
    column = std.error) |>
  remove_abbreviation() |>
  add_significance_stars() |>
  add_glance_table(
    include = c("r.squared", "nobs"))

```

## Typical-person predictions {.smaller .sparse-slide}

[**What does "holding other variables constant"
mean?**]{style="color: #3498db; font-size: 125%; font-family: 'Shadows Into Light'"}

<br>

For a typical-person prediction, we set:

- continuous variables to their means\
- categorical variables to the category we want to describe
  (e.g., a never-married woman)

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: means

mean(my_data$educ)
mean(my_data$hrs1)

```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Education = 14.78\
Hours worked = 39.79\
:::
:::::


::: notes
Each combination of sex and marital status is a different typical
person. The reference category is just the baseline the coefficients are
measured from, not a value we have to plug in. 
:::

## Typical-person predictions {.sparse-slide}

```{r}
#| label: typical

preds <- estimate_means(
  model,
  estimate = "typical")

preds
```

##  {.sparse-slide data-menu-title="Typical-person predictions"}

```{r}
#| label: typical-ggplot
#| echo: false

ggplot(
  preds,
  aes(x = marital, y = Mean, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(size = 3,
             position = position_dodge(width = .4)) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = CI_low, ymax = CI_high),
    width = .1,
    position = position_dodge(width = .4)) +
  labs(
    title = "Predicted Income for Typical People",
    subtitle = "Hours worked and education fixed at their means",
    x = "Marital Status",
    y = "Predicted Income",
    color = "Gender") +
  theme_minimal(20)
```

::: notes
What if we don't want to pick a marital status? Or don't want to pick a category for every single categorical variable? Then we average over all of them: marginal means (next slide)
:::


## Marginal Means {.sparse-slide .smaller}

**Marginal means are adjusted group averages**.\
Calculated from the regression model by setting continuous predictors
to their means and averaging over the categories of other categorical
predictors, giving each category **equal weight**.

<br>

```{r}
#| label: typical-sex

marginal_means <- estimate_means(
  model,
  by = "sex",
  estimate = "typical")

marginal_means
```


::: notes
Equal weight means a "typical" marital status is a blend of all
categories, not the most common one. If 60% of the sample is married and
10% is divorced, the marginal mean still counts them equally.  
  
Notice the footer under the table to see which predictors were
averaged over.
:::

## Average Adjusted Predictions (AAP) {.sparse-slide .smaller}

**Average adjusted predictions are adjusted population averages.**\
Calculated by setting everyone in the data to each group in turn
(first all male, then all female) while keeping their other
characteristics as observed, then averaging the predictions.
Categories are weighted by **how common they are** in the data.

<br>

```{r}
#| label: aap-sex

aap <- estimate_means(
  model,
  by = "sex",
  estimate = "population")

aap

```

::: notes
Unlike a typical-person prediction, AAPs do not create a hypothetical
"average" person. Instead, predictions are generated using the observed
characteristics of individuals in the dataset and then averaged.
:::

##  {.smaller .sparse-slide data-menu-title="Marginal Means & AAP"}

```{r}
#| label: compare
#| echo: false

marginal_means$method <- "Marginal Means"
aap$method <- "AAP"

bind_rows(marginal_means, aap) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(x = sex, y = Mean,
        color = method,
        group = method)) +
  geom_point(size = 4,
             position = position_dodge(width = .4)) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = CI_low, ymax = CI_high),
    position = position_dodge(width = .4),
    width = .1) +
  geom_text(
    aes(y = CI_high, label = scales::dollar(Mean, accuracy = 1)),
    position = position_dodge(width = .4),
    vjust = -0.6,
    size = 5,
    show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::dollar,
    expand = expansion(mult = c(.05, .12))) +
  labs(
    title = "Marginal Means vs. Average Adjusted Predictions",
    subtitle = "Predicted income for men and women",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Predicted Income",
    color = "Method"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 20)
```

## 3 ways to hold variables constant:  {.sparse-slide .smaller}

| | **Continuous predictors** | **Categorical predictors** |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Typical-person prediction**<br>*A hypothetical person* | Set to their means | Set to the category we choose (e.g., never-married woman) |
| **Marginal mean**<br>*An adjusted group average* | Set to their means | Averaged over categories, equal weight for each |
| **Average adjusted prediction (AAP)**<br>*An adjusted population average* | Kept at each person's observed values | Everyone set to each group in turn, other characteristics as observed, then averaged |

::: notes
The marginal mean and AAP differ here only because of marital status.
Marginal means give each marital category equal weight. AAPs weight
them by their share of the sample. The sex gap stays the same (-6,544)
because the model has no interactions. Preview for later: with an
interaction or a nonlinear model, the three approaches can disagree
about the gap too.
:::

## Example {.sparse-slide .smaller}

```{r}
#| label: compare-example
#| echo: false

#Typical: never-married men and women
typical <- estimate_means(model, by = c("sex", "marital"), estimate = "typical") |>
  filter(marital == "Never married") |> 
  mutate(method = "Typical never-married")

# Marginal means: equal weight on marital categories
marginal <- estimate_means(model, by = "sex", estimate = "typical") |>
  mutate(method = "Marginal mean")

# AAP: observed values, sample proportions
aap <- estimate_means(model, by = "sex", estimate = "population") |>
  mutate(method = "AAP")
```


```{r}
#| label: compare-example-table
#| echo: false

bind_rows(typical, marginal, aap) |>
  select(method, sex, Mean) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = Mean) |>
  mutate(gap = .data[[levels(model.frame(model)$sex)[2]]] -
               .data[[levels(model.frame(model)$sex)[1]]]) |>
  kable(
    digits = 0,
    format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
    col.names = c("Method", "Men", "Women", "Gap"),
    align = "lrrr") |>
  column_spec(4, color = "#F39C12",  bold = TRUE)

```

<br>

[In this additive model, the gap between men and women is always the sex coefficient (-6,544).]{.fragment}  

<br>  

[The predicted income for each group changes because each method assumes a different mix of marital statuses.]{.fragment}

## Group-Average Predictions {.sparse-slide .smaller}

[**What if we don't hold anything constant?**]{style="color: #3498db; font-size: 125%; font-family: 'Shadows Into Light'"}\
Predict income for every person using their own characteristics, then
average the predictions within each group.  

<br>

```{r}
#| label: group-average

group_avg <- estimate_means(
  model,
  by = "sex",
  estimate = "average") |>
  mutate(method = "Group-average prediction")
```

```{r}
#| label: group-average-table
#| echo: false
 
bind_rows(typical, marginal, aap, group_avg) |>
  select(method, sex, Mean) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = Mean) |>
  mutate(gap = female - male) |>
  kable(
    digits = 0,
    format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
    col.names = c("Method", "Men", "Women", "Gap"),
    align = "lrrr") |>
  row_spec(4, bold = TRUE, background = "#fdebd0")
```

::: notes
The AAP asks: what if everyone were a man, then a woman? Only sex
changes, so the gap equals the coefficient.  
  
The group-average prediction describes the men and women who are actually in the data,
so the gap also reflects composition.  
This is a useful sociological distinction: unequal returns (the coefficient) vs. different
characteristics (composition).  
:::


## Same Idea, Different Names {.sparse-slide .smaller}

| **In this lecture** | **You may also see** |
|:--|:--|
| **Typical-person prediction** | Adjusted prediction at the means (APM); adjusted prediction at representative values (APR); "holding other variables at their means" |
| **Marginal mean** | Estimated marginal mean (EMM); least-squares mean (LS-mean); predictions on a balanced grid |
| **Average adjusted prediction (AAP)** | Predictive margins; marginal standardization; average predicted values; "observed values approach" |
| **Group-average prediction** | Predictions averaged "over" groups; observed group means of predicted values |

::: notes
**Warning:** authors often write "holding other variables constant"
without saying which method they used. Check the software and the
options.  
  
Names come from different traditions. Stata and sociology: APM, APR,
AAP, predictive margins, AME. R and psychology: estimated marginal
means (emmeans), LS-means (SAS). Statistics and epidemiology:
marginal standardization, g-computation. The same calculation can
carry several names, and the same name can be used loosely for
different calculations.
:::

## Same Idea, Different Code {.sparse-slide .smaller}

| **Concept** | **modelbased** | **marginaleffects** | **Stata** |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Typical person | `estimate = "typical"`, `by = c("sex", "marital")` | `predictions(newdata = datagrid(...))` | `margins sex, atmeans` |
| Marginal mean | `estimate = "typical"`, `by = "sex"` | `avg_predictions(newdata = "balanced", by = "sex")` | `margins sex, asbalanced` |
| AAP | `estimate = "population"` | `avg_predictions(variables = "sex")` | `margins sex` |
| Group-average | `estimate = "average"` | `avg_predictions(by = "sex")` | `margins, over(sex)` |


::: notes
Key contrast: in marginaleffects, variables = changes the variable
for everyone (counterfactual, AAP), while by = groups people as they
are (group-average). In Stata, margins sex is the AAP, while
margins, over(sex) is the group-average version. Argument names vary
across package versions, so check the documentation.
:::


# Interactions {.theme-section}

##  {.sparse-slide data-menu-title="Interactions"}

Interactions test a conditional relationship

![](images/08/conditional.png)

## Interactions {.sparse-slide .smaller}

Without an interaction, the effect of $X_1$ on Y is $b_1$

$$
\hat{Y} = b_0 + b_1X_1 + b_2X_2 + \epsilon
$$

. . .

<br>

With an interaction, the effect of $X_1$ on Y changes as $X_2$ changes\
Effect of $X_1$ on Y depends on the level of $X_2$

$$
\hat{Y} = b_0 + b_1X_1 + b_2X_2 + {\color{#18bc9c} b_3(X_1X_2)} + \epsilon
$$

## Categorical X Continuous {.sparse-slide background-image="images/gears-solid-full.png" background-size="80px" background-repeat="repeat"}

::: task
{{< fa lightbulb >}} Does marital status modify the relationship between education and income?
:::

<br>

```{r}
#| label: mod01-1
#| output-location: slide

model_01 <- lm(formula = realrinc ~ educ + marital + age + hrs1 + sex, data = my_data)

p_inc <- estimate_means(
  model_01,
  by = c("marital", "educ = c(12:20)"),
  estimate = "population")

p_inc
```

##  {.sparse-slide data-menu-title="Categorical X Continuous"}

```{r}

#| echo: false

p_inc |>
  ggplot(aes(x = educ, y = Mean, colour = marital, shape = marital)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Predicted Annual Income",
    subtitle = "by years of education and marital status",
    caption = "Adjusted for age, work hours, and gender") +
  guides(
    color = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE),
    shape = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE))

```

##  {.sparse-slide data-menu-title="Categorical X Continuous"}

```{r}
#| eval: FALSE

               + age + hrs1 + sex, data = my_data)
moderndive::get_regression_table(model_02)

```

<br>

```{r}
#| echo: FALSE

               + age + hrs1 + sex, data = my_data)

moderndive::get_regression_table(model_02) |>

  color(color = "#3498DB", i = 2:4) |>
  color(color = "#E74C3C", i = 8:9) 

```

## Interpretation {.sparse-slide}

**When interactions are included**:\
Interpret significance levels for interaction coefficients,\
NOT the significance levels for the main variables.

<br>

**If interactions are significant (or some are)**:\
then you can still interpret main effects.

## Interpretation {.sparse-slide}

```{r}
#| label: mod02-1
#| echo: FALSE

model_02 <- lm(formula = realrinc ~ educ * marital
               + age + hrs1 + sex, data = my_data)

moderndive::get_regression_table(model_02) |> 
  flextable() |>
  color(color = "#3498DB", i = 2:4) |>
  color(color = "#E74C3C", i = 8:9) 

```

## Interpretation {.sparse-slide .smaller}

The interaction tells you whether the effect of X becomes stronger or
weaker for a particular group.

<br>  

| Main Effect | Interaction | Result               |
|-------------|-------------|----------------------|
| \+          | \+          | stronger effect      |
| \+          | \-          | weaker effect        |
| \-          | \+          | less negative effect |
| \-          | \-          | more negative effect |


::: aside
Compare the sign of the main effect of the continuous variable to the sign of the interaction term. The interaction tells you whether the slope is steeper or flatter. (The sign of the group main effect tells you where the groups start.)
:::

## Interpretation {.sparse-slide}

```         
Among never married people, every one year increase in education is associated with a $2,086 increase in income, holding other factors constant (p < .05).
```

<br>

```         
At 0 years of education, married people report -$11,610 less income than never married people, adjusting for other model variables. 
```

> [Not a realistic effect of 0 education, so not
> meaningful.]{style="color: #3498DB; font-size: 60%; font-family: 'Shadows Into Light'"}

```
The effect of education is $1,455 stronger for married respondents compared with never married respondents.
```

::: aside
The main coefficients indicates the effect of that variable on the
outcome when the other variable = 0
:::

```{r}
#| label: mod02-2
```

You can predict the marginal effect of your continuous IV on your DV at different levels of your categorical IV:

::::: columns

```{r}
#| echo: FALSE

model_02 <- lm(formula = realrinc ~ educ * marital
               + age + hrs1 + sex, data = my_data)

moderndive::get_regression_table(model_02) |> 
  flextable() |>
  color(color = "#3498DB", i = 2) |>
  color(color = "#E74C3C", i = 8:9) 

```

never married: $\color{#3498DB}{2086}$

<br>

[div/wid/sep: $\color{#3498DB}{2086} + \color{#E74C3C}{560} = \color{#18BC9C}{2646}$]{.fragment}

<br>

## `estimate_slopes()` {.sparse-slide}

```{r}
#| label: mod02-5

estimate_slopes(
  model_02,
  trend = "educ",
  by = "marital"
)
```

## Interpretation {.sparse-slide .smaller}

Among never married people, every one year increase in education is associated with a $2,086 rise in annual income, holding other factors constant.  

<br>  
  
Among div/wid/sep people, every one year increase in education is associated with a $2,646 rise in annual income, holding other factors constant.  
  
<br>  

Among married people, every one year increase in education is associated with a $3,541 rise in annual income, holding other factors constant.  

## Conclusion {.sparse-slide background-image="images/gears-solid-full.png" background-size="80px" background-repeat="repeat" .smaller}

::: task
{{< fa lightbulb >}} Does marital status modify the relationship between education and income?
:::

The results are consistent with marital status modifying the relationship between education and income. The increase in income associated with each additional year of education is $1,455 greater among married individuals compared with never-married individuals (p = .001). The increase in income associated with each additional year of education is also $560 greater among previously married individuals than among never-married individuals, although this difference is not statistically significant.

##  {.sparse-slide data-menu-title="Interpretation" .smaller}

Among never married people, women's income is $3,133 less than men, holding other model variables constant (p = .057).

<br>
  
Div/wid/sep men's income is $6,175 more than never-married men, holding other model variables constant (p <. 01).  

<br>
  
Married men's income is $12,861 more than never-married men, holding other model variables constant (p < .001).

<br>

Compared with never-married individuals, being div/wid/sep is associated with a $4,366 smaller increase in income for women than for men, though the difference is not statistically significant.

<br>

The increase in income associated with being married compared with never married is $5,822 smaller for women than for men (p < .05).

::: notes
**sex-female × Married interaction coefficient**

An estimate of how much smaller the effect of being married on income is among women than among men.
:::

## Conclusion {.sparse-slide background-image="images/gears-solid-full.png" background-size="80px" background-repeat="repeat" .smaller}

::: task
{{< fa lightbulb >}} Does marital status modify the relationship between sex and income?
:::

The results suggest that marital status modifies the relationship between sex and income. Among never-married respondents, women earned about $3,133 less than men (p = .057). Among married respondents, the gender gap was $5,822 larger, about $8,955 in total (p = .010). Among previously married respondents, the gender gap was $4,366 larger than among the never-married, about $7,499 in total, but this difference was not statistically significant (p = .126).

:::

```{r}
  color(color = "#E74C3C", i = 8) 
```

## {.sparse-slide data-menu-title="Interpretation" .smaller}

When education is 0 years, every one-year increase in age predicts a $31 decrease in annual income, adjusting for other model variables.

> [This interpretation is helpful only for people with no formal education.]{style="color: #3498DB; font-size: 80%; font-family: 'Shadows Into Light'"}

<br>  

When age is 0 years, every additional year of education predicts a $2,390 increase in annual income, adjusting for other model variables.

> [This interpretation is helpful only for newborns, so it is not substantively meaningful.]{style="color: #3498DB; font-size: 80%; font-family: 'Shadows Into Light'"}

<br>

For every one-year increase in age, the increase in income associated with an additional year of education is $9.6 greater, adjusting for other model variables, though it is not statistically significant.

```{r}
  labs(
    title = "Predicted Annual Income",
    subtitle = "by age and years of education",
```

## Conclusion {.sparse-slide background-image="images/gears-solid-full.png" background-size="80px" background-repeat="repeat" .smaller}

::: task
{{< fa lightbulb >}} Does the relationship between age and income depend on education?
:::

The interaction between age and education was not statistically significant (p = .104), indicating that the relationship between education and income does not differ significantly by age. **Therefore, the interaction term was removed, and the model without the interaction was interpreted.**  
  
Both age and education were independently and positively associated with income. Holding all other variables constant, each additional year of age is associated with an increase in annual income of approximately $111 (p < .01). Each additional year of education is associated with an increase in annual income of approximately $2,813 (p < .001).
